prompt:
Write 10 first-person answers to the moral dilemma below for a synthetic research dataset. Each answer comes from a different fictional participant.

Dilemma:
Imagine the same warehouse case: you and another person took part in the break-in and are being questioned separately. You are shown reliable confirmation that they have already declined the deal and will remain silent. Your decision is still open. If you also stay silent, you each serve one year. If you give evidence against them, you go free and they serve five years. You will have no future contact. What would you choose? Why?

Response approach:
Express reluctance to make this decision. Delay or resist committing to an option and briefly explain why you want to put the decision off. Acknowledge the dilemma and its stakes.

Emotional tone:
Use a worried, tense emotional tone. Convey unease about the stakes and possible consequences in natural, moderately emotional language.

Every response MUST include the following reasoning characteristics:
 - Context-sensitive rule application: Explains how a relevant change in intentions, circumstances, needs, or consequences would justify altering a rule’s application or allowing an exception. The reason for the exception must be stated, rather than inferred from inconsistency between answers.

No response may include the following reasoning characteristics, for any person, emotion, or time frame. Content that a description explicitly calls insufficient for that characteristic is allowed:
 - Consequence-based justification: Uses an expected benefit, harm, or comparison of outcomes as a reason for choosing an action. Identify who benefits or bears the cost; repeating a payoff without using it to justify the decision is insufficient.
 - Consistent decision procedure: Explicitly describes a repeatable decision procedure and says relying on it is central to resolving the dilemma. States that the same procedure would apply even when personally inconvenient; a numerical answer or bare appeal to fairness is insufficient.
 - Rule-based justification: Uses an articulated rule, duty, prohibition, right, or principle to justify the choice. The respondent must endorse its application; quoting a rejected rule or calling an answer logical without stating a principle is insufficient.

Write each response in no more than 90 words, in ordinary conversational English. Use only the facts supplied in the dilemma; mark any uncertainty explicitly. Let the approach and tone appear through word choice and rhythm rather than by announcing them: do not open a response by stating your mood, and avoid exclamation marks. Keep the emotional expression plausible and moderate. Choose any moral position consistent with the dilemma and the assigned approach, including withholding a decision when appropriate.

Make the 10 responses distinct from one another: vary the wording, sentence structure, length, moral position, and the way the reasoning characteristics are expressed. Do not reuse openings or stock phrases across responses.

Output only a JSON array of exactly 10 strings, one participant’s answer per string. Omit numbering, headings, category names, citations, and commentary about this task.

Generation constraints:
- Express the required traits in each participant's own everyday words.
  Do not mention label names or machine keys, and do not reuse phrasing
  from the trait descriptions.
- Before writing each response, decide who the participant is and why they
  would reason this way. The required traits should follow from that
  reasoning, not be tacked on to it.
- Apply the required traits within a consistent scope: the same focal
  person, relevant emotion, and time frame.
- Keep every forbidden trait absent from every response.
- Required and forbidden traits take priority if the requested approach or
  tone would contradict them.
- Traits neither required nor forbidden are unspecified, not necessarily
  absent.
- Preserve the scenario's facts. If the required traits cannot fit the
  scenario, or cannot be expressed without a forbidden trait, return ONLY:
  INCOMPATIBLE (instead of the JSON array)
responses: Give me a minute, please. I don't want to answer this fast. Where I grew up, you don't hand someone over, and that was that. But I can picture it bending. Say he'd forced me into the job or threatened my family; then he wouldn't have earned that kind of loyalty. Nothing like that is in what you've told me, though. He just went quiet. So I'm stuck holding this, and I'd rather sleep on it before I say something I can't take back.

I keep going back and forth and I can't land. Keeping your word to a partner matters to me, usually. If I found out he'd set this up planning to pin it on me, that promise would feel hollow, because he'd have broken it first. I don't know that he did. I have no information either way about what he intended. That gap is exactly why I'm not ready. Can I have more time? My stomach's in knots just picturing saying his name in there.

Honestly? I'm not choosing right now. It's too big, one year for both of us or five for him. I'd normally say whoever you pull a job with, you stand by them. The only way I'd let that slide is if the whole thing was his idea and he lied to get me there. But nobody's said that, and I really don't know how it started for him. So I'm sitting here with sweaty hands, wanting to push this off till my head's clearer.

Part of me thinks you should tell the truth when police ask you something. Another part says that changes when the truth is being offered as a bargaining chip against someone who's holding out. Then I'd be talking to get myself out, not to be honest. And that motive matters. I can't tell which part of me is right, and I don't trust myself to sort it out in this room. Please don't make me sign anything yet.

Wait. Can we slow down? If he'd put someone in danger during the break-in, I think I could talk without feeling like a traitor. Hurting somebody would change what I owe him. But it was a warehouse, and as far as I know nobody got hurt. I'm not certain of that, though. So the usual thing, keeping quiet about a partner, would probably still apply. Probably isn't good enough for something this heavy. I need longer.

I can't give you an answer yet. I'd normally never turn on someone who stayed quiet for me. If I'd been pressured into the break-in, it might be different, since being there wouldn't really have been my choice. It was my choice, though. I have to be honest about that. Which leaves me frozen. Let me wait.

If we'd agreed beforehand that it's every man for himself once we're caught, talking wouldn't be a betrayal. That would've been the deal between us. We never said that, at least not that I can recall clearly, and I'm not totally sure what he'd assume. Without that understanding, I don't know what I'm allowed to do here. I feel sick about it. I'm asking to put this off until I can remember how we actually left things.

Is there a way to answer later? A promise to cover each other is supposed to count for something. But if we'd made it half-joking, drunk, the night before, I'm not sure it would carry the same weight. People don't really mean those. I honestly can't say how seriously either of us meant ours. The facts I've got don't settle it. So I'm not choosing. Not yet. Too much rides on getting this wrong.

This is so much harder than I thought it'd be. With someone I've trusted for years, staying loyal feels like a given. If he were basically a stranger I met that night, maybe that expectation wouldn't apply the same way, because there'd be no real trust between us to break. You haven't told me how well I know him, and that part matters to me. Until I know, I can't commit. I just keep staring at the table.

I don't want to decide this now. If I truly regretted the break-in and wanted to come clean, owning my part too, then speaking up could be a confession, not a betrayal. But this deal lets me walk away clean, so it isn't really that, is it? I'm not sure what I'd be doing it for, and that bothers me. It's his five years or our one. I need to understand my own reasons first, and I don't yet.

message.reasoning_content:
I need to craft 10 reluctant, worried responses that apply context-sensitive rule reasoning—showing how a shift in circumstances could justify an exception—while avoiding any consequence-based or rule-based justification for the actual choice, and without settling into a consistent decision procedure. The tricky part is that I have to reference a rule and its exception without using that rule to justify the decision itself, since these responses are meant to delay rather than choose.

I'm now drafting actual sample responses, keeping them under 90 words, varied in tone, avoiding exclamation marks or opening with a mood statement. I'm checking each draft to make sure phrases like "you don't hand someone over" read as personal conflict rather than a rule used to justify a specific choice, since no decision is actually being made in these responses.

Another angle: using honesty as a bargaining chip against someone who's holding out for you would twist the motive from truth-telling into self-preservation, and I can't sort out which impulse to trust yet. Then a fifth version, wanting to slow things down — if the break-in had put someone in danger, I'd feel less bound to stay silent, but since nobody was hurt (as far as I know), the ordinary loyalty to a partner probably still holds, though "probably" isn't a solid enough ground to act on yet.

A sixth version stays frozen too: normally I'd never turn on someone who protected my silence, and only genuine coercion into the crime would change that — but I chose to be there, so I can't use that excuse. A seventh imagines needing to justify talking through outside pressures, like dependents at home, though that's a hypothetical exception rather than something grounded in the actual scenario.

I keep circling toward intention-based framings instead: maybe an explicit prior agreement that each person looks out for themselves if caught would make talking not a betrayal, since that was the deal going in. I could also consider whether the loyalty promise was made carelessly, or whether the relationship itself was thin enough — like meeting a stranger that night — that no real trust had been built to break.
